title: With Latest Win, Progressive Vermont Prosecutor Looks to Double Down on Reforms
author: Piper French
content:
Sarah Fair George, one of the most durable avatars of the progressive
prosecution movement, all but secured another term on Tuesday as the top
prosecutor of Burlington, Vermont.

She narrowly prevailed over challenger Bram Kranichfeld in the Democratic
primary for Chittenden County state’s attorney, and faces no opposition in the
general election in November. Kranichfeld, who currently serves as the state’s
attorney of nearby Franklin County, sought to frame George as insufficiently
tough on low-level crime and repeat offenders. He vowed to roll back many of
her reforms, a similar dynamic to George’s [last reelection bid in 2022.
](https://boltsmag.org/vermont-reform-prosecutor-wins-after-police-union-
attacks/)

“I'm a prosecutor because I think all prosecutors should be trying to put
themselves out of work,” George said in a _Bolts_ interview following her win.

After nine years as a state’s attorney, she believes that “you can do the most
good fixing a system when you are within the system.” She added, “I'm grateful
that I've been able to get into this position…Now twice, with really clear
choices for the voters, they've continued to elect me to continue to do that.”

George was first [appointed](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/scott-appoints-
new-chittenden-county-states-attorney-3970908) as Chittenden County’s state’s
attorney in 2017, just months before nationally recognized reformer Larry
Krasner was elected as Philadelphia’s district attorney, and she has won two
elections since then. She has now outlasted other prominent reform-minded
prosecutors, some of whom were ousted by voters and replaced with tougher-on-
crime successors, such as San Francisco’s Chesa Boudin, and others, like
Chicago’s Kim Foxx, who retired.

George remains part of a [national network](https://www.federaloverreach.org/)
of reform prosecutors, including Krasner, who [easily
secured](https://boltsmag.org/larry-krasner-wins-philadelphia-primary/) a
third term last year.

During her time in office, George has championed the use of [restorative
justice](https://boltsmag.org/vermont-chittenden-county-restorative-justice/)
as an alternative to prosecution, going so far as to encourage police to send
cases directly to the county’s Community Justice Centers rather than to her
office. She [ordered her staff prosecutors](https://boltsmag.org/vermont-
prosecutor-sends-staff-to-prison-in-a-bid-to-counter-their-reflex-to-
incarcerate/) to visit a prison, hoping it would make them think twice before
seeking a long sentence. She has also held fast to “blanket policies” of
refusing to prosecute certain categories of crimes. Such policies proved
[politically troublesome](https://boltsmag.org/los-angeles-da-george-gascon-
blanket-policies/) for other progressives, who ultimately abandoned or
downgraded similar policies.

She has refused to seek cash bail under any circumstance. And she has a policy
against charging violations that result from “non-public safety-related”
traffic stops, citing data showing that such stops are often pretexual and
[racially biased](https://vtdigger.org/2020/12/18/new-data-shows-burlington-
police-used-force-against-black-individuals-at-record-rate-in-2020/), which
led to significant [reductions](https://www.acluvt.org/news/smarter-stops-
safer-roads/) in traffic stops in Burlington in 2022 and 2023, according to
the ACLU.

Her policies and other choices, like her recent decision to forego charging
most protesters who participated in an action opposing an ICE raid in South
Burlington, have
[angered](https://www.facebook.com/photo?fbid=1629717544884097&set=a.512831709906025)
police both locally and across the state. In 2022, the Burlington police union
called the traffic stop policy “disastrous.”

Still, George has been able to operate with comparatively less scrutiny in
large part because, while Chittenden is Vermont’s most populous and racially
diverse county, it is also a comparatively high income, progressive enclave.
Violent crime is generally scarce, and [even lower this
year](https://www.wcax.com/2026/02/18/burlington-police-data-shows-drop-
violent-crimes/) than the past few years.

Though Vermont has a Republican governor, Phil Scott, George has not
experienced the sort of preemption that other progressive prosecutors have
faced from right-wing state leadership; Scott, a moderate, was actually the
one who first appointed her to the position. After instituting a very similar
policy governing presumptive non-prosecution of traffic stops, Tampa’s chief
prosecutor Andrew Warren was [suspended](https://boltsmag.org/florida-
governor-suspends-prosecutor-hillsborough/) by Florida Governor Ron DeSantis.

In the 2026 race, both of George’s marquee blanket policies emerged as central
points of criticism for Kranichfeld, who accused his rival of bypassing the
legislature and making up her own laws, rather than enforcing them. He pledged
to reverse the no-bail rule on his first day in office, arguing that cash bail
is appropriate in some cases, and
[told](https://www.compassvermont.com/p/a-race-nine-years-in-the-making-
kranichfeld) _Compass Vermont_ he would “prosecute serious crimes discovered
from traffic stops” and “meet with law enforcement agencies to ensure that we
have a healthy working relationship.”

George told _Bolts_ that Kranichfeld had “taken advantage of an inaccurate
narrative” about her office’s work and said that her campaign was “focused on
giving people accurate information, giving them the policies, giving them as
much research that that we use to come up with these policies as possible.”

In a way, Kranichfeld represented a road not taken for Chittenden County: Back
in late 2016, he and George were co-workers, line prosecutors who were both
considered strong contenders for the office’s top position after their boss,
TJ Donovan, was elected as Vermont’s attorney general. Like George’s 2022
challenger, attorney Ted Kenney, Kranichfeld attracted the support of business
owners in Burlington who believed George’s policies were responsible for drug
use and low-level crime in the city.

But unlike Kenney, Kranichfeld declined to seek police union support, and the
unions didn’t weigh in on the race. He spoke of balancing “compassion” for
people struggling with mental illness and addiction and “accountability” for
repeat offenders, and supported strengthening some alternatives to
incarceration like restorative justice and diversion.

Kranichfeld ultimately fell short by a closer margin than his predecessor. He
lost 48 to 52 percent, and even beat George by about 60 votes within the city
of Burlington. He [told](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/george-wins-the-
democratic-line-for-chittenden-county-states-attorney/) local outlet _Seven
Days_ that while he was disappointed in the results, he felt his campaign had
“changed the conversation in this county around public safety.”

Krainchfeld’s decision to run in Chittenden County means that he did not seek
a full term in Franklin County. Zach Weight, a Republican, is running
unopposed to replace him as Franklin County state’s attorney.

This year’s campaign also played out in the shadow of the Trump
administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement. George’s campaign
announcement this year said prosecutors must act as an “independent firewall
for Vermont’s values,” and she has joined forces with a national group of
prosecutors who have vowed to file state charges against federal agents who
break the law locally. She has declined to prosecute nearly all people
arrested at a series of anti-ICE actions, including
[demonstrations](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/protesters-arrested-at-ice-
facility-will-not-be-charged/) at an ICE intelligence office in Williston in
both February and May, and a melee between rapid responders, ICE, and state
and local police during an immigration raid in South Burlington in March. (The
three people arrested by Burlington police during the latter incident were
[sent](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/protesters-arrested-at-ice-facility-
will-not-be-charged/) to restorative justice programs).

While George initially implemented her traffic stop policy over concerns about
[statistics showing](https://vtdigger.org/2020/12/18/new-data-shows-
burlington-police-used-force-against-black-individuals-at-record-rate-
in-2020/) Black motorists in Burlington were much more likely to get pulled
over, it has taken on new resonance amid the heightened risk of immigration
enforcement under Trump.

In mid-July, after pulling over a vehicle without a front license plate, a
Chittenden County deputy sheriff
[summoned](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/chittenden-county-deputy-
investigated-for-calling-border-patrol-during-traffic-stop/) U.S. Border
Patrol and helped the responding agents detain the two passengers, leading to
one of the passengers being detained and eventually deported by ICE. (These
actions are also a violation of Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy,
which forbids local law enforcement collaboration with ICE).

The idea behind George’s policy of not prosecuting arrests stemming from
routine traffic stops is that it’ll discourage law enforcement from making
them in the first place. But in this case, the incident happened in
neighboring Franklin County, where Kranichfeld is the prosecutor.

“If that had happened here, and there had been a criminal charge from it, we’d
have been very likely to decline it,” George said. “But the damage has already
been done.”
